title: Japan
hookLine: a Korean king sends a bronze Buddha across the sea; a divided court, and then Prince Shotoku

cards: A ship crosses the strait from Korea. On board, wrapped for the journey, is a Buddha of gilt bronze, with banners, canopies and rolls of scripture.
It's a gift from the king of Baekje, one of the Korean kingdoms from a few days ago, to the ruler of Japan. With it comes a letter praising the teaching as hard to grasp and wonderful beyond measure.
The ruler opens the gift, looks at the shining face, and does what rulers do with something new and powerful. He asks his ministers.

teach.b: Japan's old chronicle, the Nihon Shoki, tells this story in the reign of Emperor Kinmei. The image and scriptures came from Baekje, so the teaching reached Japan by way of Korea. The chronicle says the ministers split.

The Soga clan said the neighbors honor this Buddha, so should we. The Mononobe and Nakatomi clans said the land's own gods would be angered. Kinmei handed the image to the Soga chief to honor at his house, as a trial.
Then sickness swept the country, the opponents blamed the foreign Buddha, and the image was thrown into a canal.

Later, the chronicle tells of a regent, Prince Shotoku, who studied the sutras with teachers from Korea and gave the teaching a home at court. It credits him with seventeen guiding articles for officials.
The second asks that the three treasures be sincerely revered: the Buddha, the Dharma and the Sangha.
Tradition links him to the founding of temples, among them Horyuji, near Nara, and Japanese Buddhists honor him as a founding patron.

Look back at the week: Guanyin hearing the cries in China, Korea receiving a monk with scriptures, Wonhyo's sweet water, Uisang walking on, Chinul's frozen pond, the woodblocks, and now a bronze Buddha crossing the sea.
Again and again, the teaching arrived from somewhere else, met doubt or hardship, and found people to carry it.

how: Japanese Buddhists honor Prince Shotoku as an early patron of the teaching, and temples linked to him, such as Horyuji near Nara, are still places of worship and pilgrimage.

games.q: you're the emperor. a gilt bronze Buddha has arrived from Korea, and your ministers disagree about it. what do you do?
o: throw it into the sea at once.
hand it to the clan that favors it, as a trial.
make it the court's only worship.
games.why: in the Nihon Shoki, Kinmei gives the image to the Soga chief to honor as a trial. it did not go smoothly.

practice: Picture the strait between the Korean peninsula and the islands of Japan, and follow one small boat across with its shining cargo.
Then go inland to Nara, among low hills, where tomorrow's story waits, and rest there with the water still moving in your mind.

wordCard.voice: Japan. Where, the old chronicle says, a gilt bronze Buddha arrived as a gift from Korea, a court argued over it, and Prince Shotoku asked that the three treasures be revered.

orig.note: Sanskrit triratna: the three treasures, the Buddha, the Dharma and the Sangha.

carryVoice: Your line: the teaching arrives. Even a Buddha thrown into a canal didn't end the story. That's the week.
